answer:
**Don't drop out. Finish college, and only reconsider if your idea is already taking off with real users.**

Paul Graham has written about this directly, and his answer is clear:

- **"Do not start a startup in college."** That line is from "Before the Startup," based on a talk he gave to students. He says that at 20, "most people should still be searching breadth-first," and that deliberately starting a startup at that age is "gratuitously stupid."
- **You can't really do both.** He writes: "You can't start a startup for real as a student, because if you start a startup for real you're not a student anymore." So dropping out isn't a separate decision. It's what happens once the company becomes real. The question is whether it has become real yet.
- **Wait unless you're sure.** In his talk to MIT students, he says YC's "party line" became to tell people "to wait till they graduate," and that YC would "only fund undergrads we can't talk out of it." He also says "if you're not certain, you should wait," because the opportunities "are not going to be gone if you don't do it now." He thinks the mid-twenties are the best age to start.
- **Use college to learn.** His advice for college is to "learn powerful things," to treat it as "education for its own sake," and to stop worrying about grades, since "users don't care what your GPA was." Good startup ideas tend to come out of that kind of learning without you trying to think them up.
- **The one exception.** He says "the best startups almost have to start as side projects," like Apple, Google, Yahoo and Facebook. If a side project starts growing like Facebook did, "it may be reasonable to run with it."

**What to do now:** stay enrolled and build the idea as a side project, or over a summer. He points out that a summer startup "reads to everyone as a summer job," so failing costs you little. Decide based on what users do, not on how excited you feel. If people are signing up, using it, and pulling it forward faster than you can keep up while in school, that's his exception, and leaving makes sense. If you just have an idea, it isn't the exception. In his words, "Just not now."

One thing he points out himself: Sam Altman left after sophomore year to found Loopt, but Graham calls him "a very unusual guy." Being a sophomore with an idea doesn't put you in that category on its own.

Sources:
- [Paul Graham, "Before the Startup"](https://paulgraham.com/before.html)
- [Paul Graham, "A Student's Guide to Startups" (MIT talk)](https://paulgraham.com/mit.html)
- [Paul Graham, "What You'll Wish You'd Known"](https://paulgraham.com/hs.html)

I'll pick bootstrapping, with one adjustment: don't wait for a lot of revenue. Paul Graham's answer would be to get to **ramen profitable** first, then raise money because you've chosen to, not because you have to.

**Why he would say that:**

1. **Ramen profitability puts you in control of the timing.** Ramen profitable means the company "makes just enough to pay the founders' living expenses." His point about it: "You can still raise money, but you don't have to do it now." If you're still losing money, "eventually you'll either have to raise more or shut down." This is the main reason I'm picking it.

2. **Investors use your need against you.** "If investors know you need money, they'll sometimes take advantage of you. Some may even deliberately stall, because they know that as you run out of money you'll become increasingly pliable." A startup that already pays its founders can negotiate harder and walk away from bad terms.

3. **Fundraising should never be your only plan.** In *Default Alive or Default Dead* he warns that "investors are so fickle that you can never do more than start to count on them," and that "you can never safely treat fundraising as more than a plan A." If your plan only works once you've raised, you're betting the company on investors following through.

4. **He also recommends this when you do raise.** In *How to Raise Money* he says "the best thing you can do is get yourself to the point where you don't need to." The pitch he wants founders to be able to make is: "We'll succeed no matter what, but raising money will help us do it faster."

5. **Fundraising takes time away from the product.** "Raising money is terribly distracting." Also: "If you don't need to raise money, you don't have to interrupt working on the company to do it."

**When he'd say raise now instead:** "Don't raise money unless you want it and it wants you." If you're already growing fast, investors are approaching you, and money would clearly speed things up, take it. Raise just "enough money to reach the speed where you can shift into the next gear," and hire slowly, since "hiring too fast is by far the biggest killer of startups that raise money." If you'd have to push skeptical investors to get a round, don't do it yet. A failed raise wastes months and hurts your reputation with investors.

**What to do:** Keep costs very low ("for a startup, cheapness is power"). Charge users as early as you can, until revenue covers the founders' rent and food. Then raise a seed round with growth to show and a business that doesn't depend on it.

Sources:
- [Ramen Profitable – Paul Graham](https://paulgraham.com/ramenprofitable.html)
- [How to Raise Money – Paul Graham](https://paulgraham.com/fr.html)
- [Default Alive or Default Dead? – Paul Graham](https://paulgraham.com/aord.html)
- [How to Fund a Startup – Paul Graham](https://paulgraham.com/startupfunding.html)

Graham's answer would be: **go to San Francisco.** He has said so consistently for almost 20 years, and Berlin doesn't change it. If you want to come back to Berlin later, he's fine with that. He wouldn't want you to skip the trip.

**What he has said and written**

- **"Why to Move to a Startup Hub" (2007):** He argues that "the more of a startup hub a place is, the better startups will do there." His reasons are that the investors are more aggressive and quicker to decide, deals happen face to face, and startups are "a very specialized business, as specialized as diamond cutting," so the expertise sits in one place. He also says the gap between the top hub and the second one is huge. Berlin isn't even the second.
- **"Cities and Ambition" (2008):** Each city sends a message about what matters. Silicon Valley's message is "how much effect you have on the world." He also writes that "you get discouraged when no one around you cares about the same things you do." He suggests trying several cities while you're young, because you only learn a city's message by living there.
- **Stockholm talk (2026):** Asked about European founders, he told them to go to Silicon Valley, even "for a bit and then come back." He said that also strengthens the home ecosystem. He cited YC data showing that companies which go home after the program have been about half as likely to become unicorns as those that stay. He was careful to say this is a correlation and doesn't prove location alone causes it.
- **On X:** He amplified a post by a founder arguing that the main reason to move to SF isn't fundraising. It's that the city raises your ambitions, because people there attempt things that would sound crazy back home. I only saw this through secondhand summaries, so check the original post before quoting it.

**When he says staying is acceptable**

The 2007 essay names four cases:

1. You'd have to uproot a family.
2. Visa problems would eat time the startup can't spare.
3. Your industry's centre is somewhere else.
4. You have a definite funding offer that depends on staying. Vague interest from an investor who "merely seems like he will fund you" doesn't count.

**My call:** If none of those four apply to you, move to SF now, during the stage when speed, fundraising and peers matter most. Stay at least until you've raised and have real traction. Graham explicitly blesses moving back to Berlin later. If one of the exceptions does apply, stay in Berlin, but make regular long trips to SF so you aren't just competing on Berlin's terms.

Most of what I found on the Stockholm talk comes from summaries, not a transcript. The full talk is on YC's YouTube channel if you want his exact words.

If Paul Graham were answering, I think he'd say you're arguing about the wrong thing. To him, persisting means sticking with the company. It doesn't mean sticking with your current idea. Unless you can point to a handful of users who really love what you have now, he'd side with your co-founder: change the idea, and keep the company and the partnership.

**Why he'd lean that way**

1. **Be stubborn about the goal, not the plan.** His essay "The Right Kind of Stubborn" says: *"The persistent are attached to the goal. The obstinate are attached to their ideas about how to reach it."* He also writes that *"persistence often requires that one change one's mind."* He says *"Mere obstinacy… is a recipe for failure,"* partly because people tend to cling to their first ideas, which are the ones least informed by experience. If what you want to keep is the current idea, he'd call that obstinacy.

2. **The first plan is usually wrong.** In "The 18 Mistakes That Kill Startups" he writes: *"Don't get too attached to your original plan, because it's probably wrong… You have to be prepared to see the better idea when it arrives."* In "How Not to Die": *"Startups almost never get it right the first time,"* and the ones that survive *"may have to morph themselves into something totally different, but they won't just crawl off and die."*

3. **A founder leaving is one of the two ways startups die.** He says the official cause of death is *"always either running out of money or a critical founder bailing,"* and the cause underneath is usually that the founders *"have become demoralized."* He also notes that about 20% of YC startups had a founder leave. If you win this argument and your co-founder quits, you've traded a pivot for one of the two things that kill startups.

**When he'd tell you to keep going**

He also warns that *"switching to a new idea every week will be equally fatal,"* and he says it's *"good for your morale to have even a handful of users who really love you."* So use this test. If some real users love the current product, and your co-founder is just worn out after a hard stretch, keep going: *"Startups rarely die in mid keystroke. So keep typing!"* If you can't name those users, the evidence is with your co-founder.

**What to do**

Sit down together and look at the user data, not at how attached either of you is to the idea. Take your co-founder's case seriously. Graham's sign of a persistent person is someone who is *"never more engaged than when you disagree with them."* Whatever you decide, decide it together. In his view, quitting is the only real failure, and a pivot isn't quitting.

Sources:

- [Paul Graham, "The 18 Mistakes That Kill Startups"](https://paulgraham.com/startupmistakes.html)

**Launch the tiny version this week.** Paul Graham's essays come down clearly on this side.

**What he's said**

- **Launching slowly kills far more startups than launching early.** In *The 18 Mistakes That Kill Startups* he writes: "Launching too slowly has probably killed a hundred times more startups than launching too fast." He lists slow launching as its own mistake and says the fix is "forcing yourself to launch *something* fairly quickly."
- **The first version doesn't need to be complete.** Early adopters "don't expect a newly launched product to do everything; it just has to do *something*." His method is to find a core that is "(a) useful on its own and (b) something that can be incrementally expanded" into the full product, then get that core out "as soon as possible."
- **Launching shows you what to build.** In *Startups in 13 Sentences*: "Launching teaches you what you should have been building." Also, "Launch fast and iterate," because "most of the ideas appear in the implementing." In *Mistakes* he adds that "it's only by bouncing your idea off users that you fully understand it." A full-featured product built before launch is mostly guesses that users haven't tested.
- **The launch can be small.** *Do Things That Don't Scale* says to get "something in front of users as soon as it has a quantum of utility, and then see what they do with it." It also says "All you need from a launch is some initial core of users." So you don't need a big public launch. You need a few real users, and he says to recruit them by hand.
- **You can do some of it manually.** He says you can "get away with doing by hand things that you plan to automate later," as Stripe's founders did when they set up merchant accounts for early users themselves. A feature you're missing could be something you do by hand for your first users.

**His one caveat:** it's "possible to launch too fast" if a broken product hurts your reputation. That's a reason to make the small version actually work, not to keep adding features.

**What to do:** pick the one thing your product does that's useful by itself. Ship it this week to a small group of users you contact yourself. Watch what they do with it, and build the next features based on that.

**Start the startup now.** If you aren't ready to found one yet, go work at a startup. Graham's writing doesn't support "go to Google for a few years to learn."

## What Graham actually says

**He used to give the "work somewhere first" advice and then dropped it.** In *Why to Not Not Start a Startup* (March 2007) he says he once told people to work for a few years first. He changed his mind after watching the founders YC funded. His conclusion: "if you're too inexperienced to start a startup, what you should do is start one," and "now I'd advise people to go ahead and start startups right out of college." He also warns that "getting a normal job may actually make you less able to start a startup." About the Kiko founders, he writes that "there is no way they'd have grown so much if they'd spent that year working at Microsoft, or even Google."

**He thinks Google is where would-be founders get stuck.** In *A Student's Guide to Startups* he calls Google a black hole: "zero startups come out of there," because "people seem to like working at Google too much to leave." His point is that a pleasant employer can "lull you into staying indefinitely." That's a local maximum, and you never build up the energy to leave. A plan of "a few years at Google" tends to turn into many more.

**Failing at a startup isn't the career risk you might think.** Graham says he asked managers at big companies, and they "said they'd prefer to hire someone who'd tried to start a startup and failed" over someone who spent the same time at a big company. As he says, the Google job "will still be waiting" if you need it.

**If you want to learn first, learn at a startup.** "The best place to work, if you want to start a startup, is probably a startup." It teaches you the right things, and it ends quickly, whether it succeeds, gets acquired or fails. More recently he has argued that a startup job beats a big-company job even if the startup fails, because your colleagues may end up running everything. That last point comes from secondhand coverage. I couldn't load the original article.

## The caveats he'd raise

- **Are you ready inside?** His test isn't age or experience. It's whether you've lost the "kid flake reflex." When someone tells you an idea is stupid, do you ask "Why do you think so?" or do you back away?
- **If you're truly unsure, wait.** In the student guide, YC's policy is "only to fund undergrads we can't talk out of it." If you can be talked out of it, you aren't ready. Even then, he'd send you to a startup, not Google.
- **The timing argues for now.** He puts the sweet spot in the mid-twenties: you have stamina, low costs, few ties and easy access to co-founders. Each year at a comfortable big company uses up those advantages.

## The bottom line

Graham's view is that founding a company is the fastest way to learn how to found one. Google teaches big-company habits and pays you well to keep them. Start now if you can. If you can't yet, join an early-stage startup.

Sources:

- [Paul Graham, "A Student's Guide to Startups"](https://paulgraham.com/mit.html)

**Pick the hard, ambitious idea, but don't start by building the whole thing. Start with a small first version that some people want badly right now, and expect it to make a little money early.** That's what Paul Graham's own essays point to. He doesn't really accept "money now vs. ambitious later" as a choice. In his view the ambitious path *starts* with something small that works.

**Why the ambitious idea wins**
- In "Frighteningly Ambitious Startup Ideas" he says the biggest ideas scare people off because "they threaten your identity: you wonder if you'd have enough ambition to carry them through." People's minds filter those ideas out. If one is scaring you, it may be the one worth doing.
- In "How to Get Startup Ideas," the best ideas are ones you want yourself, can build yourself, and that few others see the value in. A hard idea that takes years is more likely to clear that last bar than another AI tool that makes money quickly.
- In "How to Do Great Work," he says to work on "whatever seems to you excitingly ambitious" and lists money among the things that pull people off course. His answer to that pull is to "stick to what you find genuinely interesting."

**Why you shouldn't attack it head-on**
- From the same ambitious-ideas essay: "Even the most ambitious people are probably best off approaching them obliquely… the way to do really big things seems to be to start with deceptively small things." And: "Don't try to construct the future like a building, because your current blueprint is almost certainly mistaken."
- His examples: Microsoft's first product was Altair BASIC, and Facebook started for Harvard students only. He calls that "a well": something narrow and deep that a few people want a lot.

**Where making money fits**
- In "Ramen Profitable," he says covering your living costs matters because "it buys you time" and means "you're no longer at the mercy of investors." He also says it "is not the destination," just "a trick for not dying en route."
- He warns that side work that pays the bills "might turn you into a consulting firm," because consulting "just can't scale the way a product can." So don't build an unrelated money-making AI tool on the side. Make your early revenue come from the first, smallest version of the big idea.

**What to do:** Find the smallest part of the hard idea that a specific group needs right now. Ship it in weeks, charge for it, and keep it going until it covers your rent. Then expand step by step toward the larger vision, as he puts it: "Start with something you know works, and when you expand, expand westward." If the AI tool you're considering can be that first version, do it. If it's a separate project you'd run just for the money, skip it.

These essays are from 2009 to 2023. The searches turned up nothing from Graham in 2026 that changes this, though he has said AI made many "almost-solvable problems" solvable. That makes a hard AI idea more practical to start small than it used to be.

**My answer is to focus on building, and that is almost certainly what Paul Graham would tell you.** Writing to work out your own thinking is fine. Writing posts to build an audience while your product isn't working yet takes the founder attention he considers most valuable. Here's what he has actually said and done.

**What he's said**
- **Founder attention is the scarcest thing you have.** In 2016 he told startups to skip Shark Tank. When Chris Sacca called that free publicity, Graham replied: *"Nothing is less free for a startup than something that costs the attention of the founders,"* and *"Building the best product is how most startups win, not by marketing."* Posting online to get attention is the same trade on a smaller scale.
- **"Avoid distractions."** It's item 10 of his "Startups in 13 Sentences": *"Nothing kills startups like distractions."* The other items that bear on this are *"Launch fast"* and *"Understand your users. That's the key."* None of the 13 say anything about building an audience.
- **"Playing house."** In "Before the Startup" he describes founders who *"imitat[e] all the outward forms of a startup"* while neglecting *"the one thing that's actually essential"*: *"You have to make something people want, and you prosper only to the extent you do."* Building a personal brand before the product works is a modern way of playing house.

**What he's done, which matters more**
- He ran Viaweb from 1995 to 1998 and only started publishing essays around 2001, after it was sold. He didn't write essays while he was the founder.
- His essays did turn into deal flow for Y Combinator. But by then he was an investor, and writing was effectively part of his job.
- Writing alongside running Hacker News became *"disastrous"* for his stress. Later, when he wanted to finish his Bel programming language, he stopped himself writing essays because otherwise *"I'd never have finished."* So even he cuts writing when there's something to ship.

**The one thing to keep:** in "Writes and Write-Nots" he says *"writing is thinking."* Keep writing for yourself: memos, notes on users, a plan you've worked through. Just don't publish it for reach.

**What to do:** spend your time building and talking to users until people clearly want the product. Write privately to get your thinking clear. Publish only when a piece directly helps you get users or hire people. Leave essay-writing for after you've won, the way Graham did.

One caveat: you'll often see "a startup should only do two things: build and talk to users" credited to Graham. I couldn't find it in his own writing, so I haven't used it as his quote.

**Stay small.** Paul Graham's position on this is about as firm as his positions get. He's written that "hiring too fast is by far the biggest killer of startups that raise money." That puts your situation, just after closing a round, at the top of his list of danger points.

**What he has said:**

- **Hiring is how funded startups die.** In *Default Alive or Default Dead?* he calls overhiring the top threat to startups that raise money. He also warns that founders who have just raised are often pushed to overhire by the VCs who funded them. Expect that pressure and don't treat it as advice you have to follow.
- **It costs you twice.** In *How Not to Die* he calls hiring "the classic way to burn through cash." It also slows you down, citing Brooks's *The Mythical Man-Month*. So you burn more money each month and make less progress, which means the money has to last longer while going faster.
- **Growth should come from the product.** At seed stage the product usually still needs to change, and he notes that's "usually easier with fewer people." His alternatives to hiring are doing things that don't scale, and redesigning the product in a way only the founders can.
- **His rules, if you must hire:** (a) don't, if you can avoid it. (b) Pay in equity rather than salary, which also attracts people who are committed. (c) Hire only people who write code or get users.
- **Money doesn't buy speed.** He writes that "more money can't get software written faster." He also says a big raise is dangerous mostly because of what comes with it: "your company moves to the suburbs and has kids."

**What to do:** treat the seed round as runway, not a hiring budget. Keep the team as small as you can, and only hire when a specific hole is limiting growth and the founders can't fill it themselves. Even then, hire one person who builds or sells, not a team. Aim to become "default alive," meaning that at your current spending and growth you'd reach profitability before the money runs out. Every hire moves that date further away.

Work on the one you're passionate about. That's very likely Paul Graham's answer too, with one condition.

**Why he'd pick it**

1. **He calls big-market-from-afar ideas "made-up" ideas.** In *Organic Startup Ideas* he splits ideas into two kinds. Some "grow organically out of your own life." Others "you decide, from afar, are going to be necessary to some class of users other than you." He says organic ideas are "generally preferable," and that "the worst ideas we see at Y Combinator are from young founders making things they think other people will want." Choosing an idea because its market is bigger is usually that second kind. YC calls them "sitcom" ideas: they sound plausible but nobody actually needs them.

2. **He doesn't care how big the market is at the start.** In *How to Get Startup Ideas* he says you can dig a hole that's "broad but shallow, or one that's narrow and deep, like a well," and tells you to choose the well. Microsoft began with Altair Basic, for "only a couple thousand Altair owners." Facebook started out "exclusively for Harvard students." What counts is a small group that wants it a lot, plus "a fast path out" to something bigger. A large market where people only want your product a little loses to that.

3. **Interest makes you work harder.** In *How to Do Great Work* he writes "When in doubt, optimize for interestingness" and "Interest will drive you to work harder than mere diligence ever could." He lists "money" and "fashion" among the things that pull people off course.

**The condition**

To him, "passion" means you want the thing yourself, not just that you like the topic. His three tests for the best ideas: "something the founders themselves want, that they themselves can build, and that few others realize are worth doing." So check your passion idea against them. Do you, or a few people you know, want it badly right now? Could you build it? Is there a believable way to grow from that small group to a bigger one? If yes, build it, and don't let the size of the other market tempt you. If you only find the subject fun and nobody urgently needs the product, it's also a sitcom idea. In that case, look for a problem you actually have instead.

His one-line version: "Live in the future and build what seems interesting."

Sources:
- [Paul Graham, "How to Get Startup Ideas"](https://paulgraham.com/startupideas.html)
- [Paul Graham, "Organic Startup Ideas"](https://paulgraham.com/organic.html)
- [Paul Graham, "How to Do Great Work"](https://paulgraham.com/greatwork.html)

I've finished searching Paul Graham's essays. Here's the answer.

## Apply to Y Combinator

Paul Graham would almost certainly tell you to apply to YC, and his reasoning is about math more than loyalty. Keep in mind that he co-founded YC, so he isn't neutral. Here is his case, built from his own essays. None of them compares the two options head to head.

**1. Do the equity math.** In "The Equity Equation," Graham says to give up a fraction *n* of your company only if the deal makes the company worth more than 1/(1−n). For YC's 7%, the bar is 1.075. If YC raises your company's expected outcome by more than 7.5%, you come out ahead. He adds that anyone who thinks YC is a bad deal must believe it can't improve a startup's odds by even 7.5%. Ask yourself honestly whether three months of coaching, the network and Demo Day would add 7.5% to your outcome. For most first-time founders the answer is clearly yes.

**2. The first check is the hardest part, and YC solves it.** In "How to Raise Money" he writes that "getting the first substantial offer can be half the total difficulty of fundraising." He also says "the biggest factor in most investors' opinions of you is the opinion of other investors." Going straight to angels means getting through that cold start alone. YC does that step for you and then puts you in front of investors at Demo Day.

**3. Angels are harder to reach and less reliable.** In "How to Fund a Startup" he says the best way to find angels is personal introductions, while you can apply to a seed firm through its website without one. He also warns not to count on an angel's yes until the money arrives. Seed firms use standard terms, and since earlier startups signed those terms and did well, the terms are probably reasonable. Individual angels have less reputation to protect.

**4. Fundraising distracts you.** In "A Hacker's Guide to Investors" he calls raising money "a huge time suck at just the point where startups can least afford it." He also says teaching founders how to deal with investors is "probably the second most important thing we do at Y Combinator."

**When he'd say to skip both:** "Don't raise money unless you want it and it wants you." If outside money wouldn't make you grow faster, don't raise at all.

**Even with YC, collect your own introductions.** He says you should add your own leads to the Demo Day ones, because investors you find yourself "will on average be better investors." Get to know tech-savvy angels now, and raise from them after Demo Day.

**What to do:** apply to the next YC batch. If you already have strong angels lined up, run the 1/(1−n) test on them too. Unless their money comes with comparable help, YC still wins on Graham's own numbers.

**Get a co-founder first.** That's clearly Paul Graham's answer. But he'd add a condition: pick a good one, and don't grab just anyone to avoid being solo.

**What he's written:**

- **He lists going solo as startup mistake #1.** In "The 18 Mistakes That Kill Startups," the first mistake is having a single founder. He notes that few successful startups had one founder. He also calls being solo "a vote of no confidence," since it suggests you couldn't talk any of your friends into joining you. His core reason is: "Starting a startup is too hard for one person. Even if you could do all the work yourself, you need colleagues to brainstorm with, to talk you out of stupid decisions, and to cheer you up when things go wrong."
- **The emotional side matters most to him.** "The low points in a startup are so low that few could bear them alone." With co-founders, each person thinks "I can't let my friends down," which he calls "one of the most powerful forces in human nature."
- **He gives a target size.** In "How to Start a Startup": "Ideally you want between two and four founders." More than that and disagreements "harden into factions." For a tech startup, at least one founder should be technical, and someone has to be focused on what users want.
- **He ranks co-founders above the idea.** Sentence #1 of "Startups in 13 Sentences" is "Pick good cofounders." He writes that "cofounders are for a startup what location is for real estate." You can change your idea easily, but you can't really change your co-founders.
- **He says how to find them: not through networking.** Look among people you've studied or worked with. Build side projects with people you like and let a partnership grow out of that. "Don't make a conscious effort to schmooze." He pushed Drew Houston to find a co-founder before YC would fund Dropbox, and Houston recruited Arash Ferdowsi within about two weeks.

**What that means for you:** Don't wait to start building. Start the project now and use the work to recruit. Show the prototype to the smartest people you've worked or studied with and see who can't stop thinking about it. Only commit to someone you'd trust in a fight, because by his logic a bad co-founder is permanent. If you truly can't convince anyone, treat that the way he does: as a signal to look at hard, about either the idea or how you're pitching it.

One caveat: he has never said solo founders can't succeed. One Hacker News commenter quoted YC's old informal rule as "no single founders unless you're a genius," and Fortune reported that he has funded solo founders too, though teams do better on average. So going solo is possible, but by his reasoning it's the harder path.
